housing.summary: Los Angeles has an expensive, competitive rental market. Leases are typically 12 months; landlords require proof of income (often 2.5-3x rent), credit check, and references. Rents are highest on the Westside and downtown; more affordable inland.

banking.summary: Opening a US bank account typically requires an in-person visit with ID and a US taxpayer identification number. Newcomers can often open with a passport plus SSN or ITIN and proof of local address.

schools.summary: Public schools are run by the Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD), the second-largest US district; enrollment is address-based. Numerous private and international schools offer IB and other curricula.

legal_admin.summary: The US has no local residence-registration system. Foreign nationals' status is governed by their visa; immigration matters are handled federally by USCIS. New residents update their address with USCIS (AR-11) and other agencies.
legal_admin.registration_step: No municipal registration; maintain lawful immigration status and file address changes with USCIS (Form AR-11) where required

tax_finance.summary: Residents file federal taxes with the IRS and state taxes with California's Franchise Tax Board. Workers need a Social Security Number (SSN); those ineligible use an ITIN. California has state income tax in addition to federal.

transport.summary: Los Angeles is car-centric but has a growing public transit network run by LA Metro (buses and rail) using the TAP card. Foreign driving licences generally cannot be directly exchanged; residents must obtain a California licence via the DMV. There is no universal public healthcare registration.
transport.driving_licence_exchange: No direct exchange; foreign licence holders must apply for a California licence through the DMV, including written and (often) driving tests
transport.healthcare_registration: No universal healthcare registration; coverage is via employer, private insurance, or the Covered California marketplace
